evidence: We studied in situ the initial stages of atomic layer deposition (ALD) of HfO2 by an ultra high vacuum atomic force microscope working in frequency-modulation mode. The ALD cycles, made by using tetrakis-di-methylamido-Hf and water as precursors, were performed on the Si(001)/SiO2 substrate maintained at 230 °C. After each ALD cycle we studied the influence of the HfO2 growth on the surface height histogram, the root mean square roughness, the surface fractal dimension and the autocorrelation function. This detailed analysis of the surface topography allowed us to confirm the completion of the first HfO2 layer after four ALD cycles. The most commonly used parameter in AFM data analysis is Sq, which is equal to the standard deviation of the height and thus describes the spread of the HD around the mean value. Two other parameters closely related to HD are: Ssk, and Sku. Skewness describes the asymmetry of the HD and is equal to 0 for a Gaussian surface. A negative Ssk indicates a surface-porous sample with predominance of valleys or holes, while positive is seen on surfaces with islands. Kurtosis is a measure of the sharpness of the surface HD and for a Gaussian surface equals 3. Sku with values smaller than 3 indicates a broad HD that would be referred to a bumpy surface, whereas values larger than 3 refer to a surface with sharp islands or holes. The in-plane analysis was performed by calculating the ACF, determining the relationship of any point of the surface to all other points. AFM data analyzed by ACF produce 3D images. In order to obtain only one particular value of Scl parameter, the ACF was radially averaged giving rise to the radial autocorrelation function (RCF). The first minimum of the RCF corresponds to the mean distance of the similar objects. To get additional information about the spatial properties of the surface together with ACF we also used the fractal analysis by means of Sfd. Sfd can be considered as a measure of complexity of the surface and is a number between 2, for completely flat plane, and 3 for extremely rough surface. The closer is Sfd to 3, the more complex is the analyzed surface. We used two routines to calculate Sfd: cube counting (CC) method, and power spectral density (PSD) method. It can be shown that, in general, both methods give different values for Sfd parameter.
